description: First-run cursor is seeded one interval in the FUTURE instead of the past.
First-run look-back treats the interval as minutes instead of seconds (60x too far back).
Stored cursor is ignored; every run re-seeds from now - interval.
Cursor save coroutine is never awaited, so progress is never persisted.
Handlers are given the run-start snapshot (next cursor) instead of the stored/seeded cursor.
Persisted cursor is 'now' at save time instead of the snapshot taken before fetching; changes made during the fetch are skipped next run.
Leaving the cursor scope restores the wrong value, so the cursor leaks to code running after the incremental run.
A kind with a single error is treated as successful and its cursor advances.
After a kind fails the run carries on with the remaining kinds instead of halting.
A kind that partially failed (errors but some entities synced) still advances its cursor.
An exception while syncing a kind (e.g. Port rejecting the cursor write) is reported as success, so the run continues.
Kinds without an incremental handler are no longer filtered out; they fail the incremental run.
Every mapping block of a kind reads the cursor of block 0.
Block index is counted among incremental kinds only, so cursors are keyed by the wrong mapping position when full-resync-only kinds precede them.
Catch-all handlers are taken from the full-resync registry, so incremental runs also call catch-all full-resync handlers.
A successful update is followed by a create request as well.
A cursor document without a stored value crashes instead of reading as 'no cursor'.
Errors reading a cursor are swallowed and look like 'no cursor yet', silently restarting the kind from the default look-back.
Creating a cursor sends no auth headers.
Updating a cursor sends no auth headers.
Server-side filter drops the configured value prefix (e.g. '>=').
Client-side cut-off keeps the stale items and drops the fresh ones.
Server-side filter ignores the custom date format and always sends ISO 8601.
Items updated exactly at the cursor are treated as stale (off-by-one at the boundary).
Early-stop is evaluated on the filtered batch, which never contains stale items, so pagination never stops.
Cut-off strategy without sort params (API already newest-first) crashes on incremental runs.
Timestamps with a non-UTC offset are relabelled as UTC instead of converted, so they are compared against the cursor at the wrong instant.
